name: Cross Collar Choke from 3-4 Mount
description: Master the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount in BJJ. Complete guide covering grip mechanics, finishing details, and defensive counters for gi grapplers.
summary: The cross collar choke from 3-4 mount is a gi blood choke where the asymmetric mount's posted-leg base lets the attacker commit both hands to deep cross-collar grips, compressing both carotid arteries to force the tap.
overview:
The cross collar choke from 3-4 mount exploits the asymmetric weight distribution unique to this mount variation, where the top player's posted leg creates a stable platform for maintaining position while both hands work the collar grips. Unlike the standard mounted cross collar choke, the 3-4 configuration provides enhanced base stability during the grip insertion phase, reducing the risk of being swept when reaching for the second collar grip. The posted leg anchors the attacker's weight, allowing them to commit both hands to collar work without sacrificing positional control.

Strategically, this submission functions as a high-pressure finishing tool within the 3-4 mount attack chain. The choke creates a powerful dilemma for the bottom player: defending the collar grips exposes the arms to Americana and armbar attacks, while protecting the arms leaves the neck vulnerable. Advanced practitioners set up the cross collar choke as the primary threat to open secondary submissions, making it central to the 3-4 mount submission system. The gi collar serves as a natural choking mechanism, with the cross-grip configuration compressing both carotid arteries simultaneously for a blood choke finish.

The 3-4 mount also allows the attacker to use their posted leg to drive forward pressure during the finishing sequence, amplifying the choking force while maintaining balance. This makes the choke particularly dangerous against opponents who rely on bridging as their primary mount escape, since the bridge actually tightens the collar across the neck when grips are already established. Competition footage consistently shows this as a high-percentage finish at the purple belt level and above.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to temporary loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for serious injury if held past unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper hand placement centering pressure on the windpipe
injury_risks.recovery_time: 1-2 weeks for minor irritation; months for severe cartilage damage

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from defensive bridging and turning reactions under pressure

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum application time in training
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or any verbal signal)
Physical hand tap on partner's body or mat
Physical foot tap on mat or partner
Any distress signal including facial expressions or loss of resistance
release_protocol: Immediately release both collar grips upon tap signal
Open mount and disengage controlling position to allow recovery
Allow partner space to recover breathing and circulation
Check partner's alertness and ensure full recovery before continuing
training_restrictions: Never apply full choking pressure during initial learning phases - focus on grip mechanics first
Never hold the choke past the tap signal under any circumstances
Never use competition speed or intensity in basic drilling
Never practice on partners with neck or circulation issues without instructor supervision
Always ensure partner has clear access to tap with hands or feet

attacker.name: from 3-4 Mount Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to execute the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount. Detailed grip sequences, weight distribution, and finishing mechanics for gi submission attacks.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount requires systematic grip insertion combined with precise weight management. The posted leg provides a stable base that allows aggressive collar work without sacrificing mount position. Success depends on establishing the first grip deep enough to serve as an anchor, then using weight shifts and pressure changes to create the opening for the second grip. The finishing sequence uses elbow retraction and chest-to-face pressure to compress the carotid arteries, with the 3-4 mount's asymmetric base providing resistance against late-stage bridge escapes. The key tactical advantage is that both hands can commit to collar work while the posted leg maintains defensive base, a luxury unavailable in standard mount.
key_principles: Grip depth determines everything: four fingers past the first knuckle into the collar is the minimum for a competition-finishing grip
The posted leg is your insurance against sweeps - never lift or reposition it during the grip insertion phase
Weight forward through the chest compresses breathing and forces the opponent to address pressure rather than purely defending grips
Secure and consolidate the first grip completely before attempting the second - rushing creates openings for grip fighting
Forehead pressure into the opponent's jaw turns their chin and exposes collar access for the second grip
Elbow retraction toward the mat during the finish amplifies choking pressure through leverage rather than muscular strength
setup_requirements: Established 3-4 mount with inside knee tight to opponent's ribcage and posted leg providing stable base
Opponent wearing a gi with accessible collar material around the neck area
Weight distributed forward through hips to restrict opponent's breathing and movement capacity
At least one of opponent's defensive frames cleared or neutralized before reaching for the first collar grip
Opponent's chin line accessible and not buried against their chest with tight double underhook defense

execution_steps.description: Establish the 3-4 mount configuration with your inside knee tight against the opponent's ribcage and your outside leg posted for base. Distribute your weight through your hips onto their diaphragm, ensuring stable forward pressure before initiating any collar grip work.

With your posted-leg-side hand, reach across to grip their far collar at the level of their neck crease. Thread your fingers inside the collar with your thumb on the outside, pulling the lapel tight against the side of the neck. Maintain chest pressure throughout to prevent framing space.

Once the first grip is set deep, pull the collar tight across their throat to remove all slack from the material. Use your gripping arm's elbow to pin their bicep or shoulder, reducing their ability to frame. Adjust weight slightly forward to compensate for the hand position shift.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds to remove slack and settle

execution_steps.description: Drive your forehead or temple into the side of their jaw to rotate their chin away, exposing the near-side collar. Strip their defensive grips by peeling their wrists toward their hips or swimming your arm underneath their frames to access the collar material.

Slide your free hand inside the near-side collar with thumb in, matching depth with the first grip. The second hand feeds under the first arm in a cross pattern. Drive fingers deep toward the back of the neck, ensuring both grips have four fingers inside the collar past the first knuckle.
execution_steps.timing: 1-3 seconds - must be quick once opening is created

execution_steps.description: Drop your elbows toward the mat while expanding your chest outward and driving your weight forward over their face. The cross-grip configuration creates a scissoring action across both carotid arteries. Maintain steady increasing pressure without jerking or sudden force application.

Keep your hips heavy and your head low as the choke sets in. If the opponent bridges, ride with the movement while keeping collar tension constant. The posted leg drives into the mat to resist any late escape attempts. Hold steady pressure until the tap or verbal signal.

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one grip fighting to strip the first collar grip before it consolidates
common_counters.your_response: Immediately control their far-side wrist with your free hand and threaten to step over for an armbar on the grip-fighting arm, creating a dilemma between defending the choke and protecting the arm

common_counters.counter: Bridge toward posted leg during second grip insertion when both attacker hands are committed
common_counters.your_response: Post your free hand momentarily and ride the bridge while maintaining first collar grip tension; use the post-bridge settling moment to immediately reinsert the second grip as they return flat

common_counters.counter: Frame on biceps with extended arms to create distance and prevent closing the choke
common_counters.your_response: Walk your hips higher toward their head, compressing their frames under your weight; switch to armbar or mounted triangle attack if their arms remain extended and isolated

common_counters.counter: Turn away and give up the back to escape the choke pressure entirely
common_counters.your_response: Transition immediately to seat belt control or technical mount; maintain collar grips through the turn for a potential bow and arrow choke from back control

common_errors.error: Reaching for collar grips before establishing stable 3-4 mount base
common_errors.consequence: Opponent exploits the weight shift to bridge and reverse, resulting in lost mount position and potential full reversal to bottom
common_errors.correction: Settle your weight and control at least one arm before initiating any grip work; the position must be stable before the submission attempt begins

common_errors.error: Inserting grips too shallow with only fingertips on the collar surface
common_errors.consequence: Grips slip under finishing pressure, choke produces throat discomfort without blood choke effect, and opponent escapes during re-gripping attempts
common_errors.correction: Thread four fingers inside the collar past the first knuckle with palm positioned so the wrist bone contacts the carotid artery when the elbow retracts

common_errors.error: Sitting upright during the finishing sequence instead of driving weight forward
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for the opponent to bridge, reduces choking leverage through poor angle, and elevates center of gravity making sweeps easier
common_errors.correction: Drop your chest toward the opponent's face during the finish, keeping elbows tight to your body and weight driving forward and down through their sternum

common_errors.error: Rushing the second grip insertion without consolidating the first grip
common_errors.consequence: Both grips end up shallow, the first grip loosens during the second hand's insertion, and the opponent strips both grips simultaneously
common_errors.correction: Set the first grip deep, remove all collar slack, and use elbow pressure to pin their arm before reaching for the second collar

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms and biceps rather than using skeletal structure and bodyweight
common_errors.consequence: Rapid forearm fatigue within 10-15 seconds, inconsistent pressure that allows the opponent to survive and work escape sequences
common_errors.correction: Use elbow retraction toward the mat and chest expansion for choking force; think about driving elbows to the floor rather than squeezing the hands together

common_errors.error: Neglecting head position and allowing the opponent to tuck their chin toward you
common_errors.consequence: Chin tuck blocks collar access for the second grip, turns a blood choke into an ineffective jaw crank, and dramatically reduces finishing percentage
common_errors.correction: Use forehead pressure against their jaw to turn the chin away before inserting grips; maintain head pressure against the jaw throughout the entire finishing sequence

training_progressions.focus: Developing deep collar grips from 3-4 mount
training_progressions.description: Practice inserting collar grips against a fully compliant partner, focusing on hand placement depth and collar tension. Drill both first and second grip insertion 20 times each side, emphasizing finger depth past the first knuckle and thumb positioning on the outside of the collar.

training_progressions.focus: Combining collar work with mount pressure maintenance
training_progressions.description: Partner provides light resistance while you practice maintaining 3-4 mount pressure during grip insertion. Focus on keeping hips heavy while reaching for collars, using the posted leg for base throughout. Partner signals when they feel pressure relief to identify weight distribution errors.

training_progressions.focus: Reading and defeating common grip defenses
training_progressions.description: Partner applies specific defenses at 50% resistance: two-on-one grip strips, bridging during second grip, bicep frames, and chin tuck. Attacker practices identifying each defense type and applying the appropriate counter. Cycle through all defense types in random order.

training_progressions.focus: Executing the choke under realistic resistance
training_progressions.description: Start from 3-4 mount against progressive resistance building from 50% to full resistance across rounds. Attacker has 3 minutes to achieve the choke or transition to other submissions. Track success rate across rounds to identify weak points in the attack chain.

training_progressions.focus: Using the choke threat to open secondary attacks
training_progressions.description: Practice the cross collar choke as the primary threat while transitioning to armbars, Americanas, and mounted triangles when defenses create openings. Develop the ability to flow between submissions based on defensive reactions without abandoning mount position.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The cross collar choke attacks both carotid arteries simultaneously through a scissoring compression created by the cross-grip collar configuration. The wrists and forearm bones create bilateral pressure points on either side of the neck, restricting blood flow to the brain. The lapel material concentrates force on the carotid triangles, making this a blood choke rather than an airway choke when applied correctly with proper wrist positioning lateral to the trachea.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins a two-on-one grip fight against your first collar grip - what adjustment prevents them from stripping it?
flashcards.answer: Immediately use your free hand to control their far-side wrist and pin it to the mat, removing half their grip-fighting capacity. Maintain the first collar grip as an anchor and threaten to step over for an armbar on the arm reaching up to strip your grip. This creates a dilemma: they either stop grip fighting to defend the arm attack, giving you the collar back, or they continue fighting your grip and expose the armbar. The grip-fight itself becomes a submission setup.

flashcards.question: Why is the 3-4 mount configuration specifically advantageous for the cross collar choke compared to standard mount?
flashcards.answer: The 3-4 mount provides a posted leg that maintains base stability when both hands leave the mat to work collar grips. In standard mount, committing both hands to collar work eliminates all posting ability, making the attacker vulnerable to bridge and roll escapes. The posted leg in 3-4 mount acts as an anchor against the bridge direction, allowing the attacker to focus entirely on grip work while maintaining defensive base through the lower body structure.

flashcards.question: You have both collar grips set deep but the opponent is bridging hard toward your posted leg - how do you maintain the choke?
flashcards.answer: Ride the bridge by shifting your weight in the same direction while maintaining collar tension. Use the momentum of their bridge to walk your hips higher on their chest, which actually improves your finishing angle. Keep your elbows tight and drive them toward the mat as the opponent settles from the bridge. The post-bridge moment when they return flat is the highest-percentage finishing window because they have expended energy and momentarily relaxed their defensive structure.

flashcards.question: What indicates the choke is properly compressing the carotid arteries rather than crushing the trachea?
flashcards.answer: A properly applied blood choke causes the opponent's face to flush red or purple within seconds, their movements become sluggish, and they may not feel immediate sharp pain. An airway choke, by contrast, causes coughing, gagging, and immediate sharp pain in the throat. If the opponent is making choking or gagging sounds, the wrists are too centered on the trachea rather than positioned on the carotid triangles on either side of the neck. Adjust wrist angle laterally to correct.

flashcards.question: Your first grip is set but you cannot get your second hand past your opponent's chin tuck - what adjustment do you make?
flashcards.answer: Drive your forehead or temple into the side of their jaw, using head pressure to rotate their chin away from the collar you are targeting. Simultaneously use your first grip to pull the collar across their neck, tightening the material and creating a crease that your second hand can follow into the collar. If chin tuck persists, drive your elbow into the gap between their chin and chest to wedge their jaw open before inserting the second grip along the exposed collar line.

flashcards.question: What are the immediate actions required if your training partner loses consciousness during a cross collar choke?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release all collar grips and positional pressure. Place the unconscious partner on their back and elevate their legs slightly to promote blood flow return to the brain. Monitor breathing and be prepared to call for medical assistance. Most blood choke unconsciousness resolves within 10-20 seconds once released, but the partner should not continue training for at least several minutes after regaining consciousness and should be monitored for confusion, headache, or other concerning symptoms.

flashcards.question: In competition, you are ahead on points with 90 seconds left and have 3-4 mount with one collar grip set - should you commit to the choke?
flashcards.answer: With a points lead, use the collar grip as a control tool and threat rather than fully committing to the finish. Maintain 3-4 mount pressure and keep the first grip deep to limit their defensive options and force them to address the choke threat. Only commit the second hand if you can do so without risking a reversal. If they begin aggressive escape attempts, the collar grip helps maintain mount control. A failed submission attempt that results in lost position could cost you the match.

flashcards.question: Your opponent has extended arms pushing on your chest to create distance - how does this affect your choke setup?
flashcards.answer: Extended arms pushing on your chest are a defensive gift disguised as resistance. Their isolated, extended arms are vulnerable to armbar, Americana, or wrist control attacks. Immediately swim one arm past their push and into the collar, or collapse their extended arm to the mat and insert your grip while passing their frame. The push creates space between their hands and their own neck, making it easier to access the collar material without fighting through tight elbow frames.

flashcards.question: What is the critical grip depth indicator that determines whether the cross collar choke can produce a finish?
flashcards.answer: The four fingers must pass at least the first knuckle inside the collar, with the palm positioned so the wrist bone applies pressure to the carotid artery when the elbow retracts. A reliable test is whether you can pull the collar tight enough to make visible contact with the opposite side of the neck. If the grip is too shallow, the collar material bunches without creating the necessary compression angle, and the choke degrades into uncomfortable pressure without achieving circulatory restriction.

defender.name: from 3-4 Mount Defender
defender.description: Defend the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount with proven grip-stripping techniques, escape timing, and guard recovery methods for bottom mount players.
defender.overview: Defending the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount requires immediate recognition of collar grip attempts and proactive hand fighting to prevent deep grip establishment. The defender's primary advantage is that the attacker must commit both hands to collar work, temporarily reducing their ability to maintain position. Timing is critical: early grip prevention is far more effective than attempting to strip established grips. The asymmetric 3-4 mount creates specific escape windows when the attacker reaches for the second collar, momentarily compromising their base on the posted leg side. Understanding the stages of the choke setup allows the defender to choose the most effective response at each phase rather than reacting to a fully locked submission.
key_principles: Grip prevention is ten times more effective than grip removal: fight the first hand before it enters the collar
Keep elbows tight to your body to maintain structural frames that prevent the attacker from closing distance to the neck
Protect your neck by tucking your chin to your chest and maintaining at least one hand near the collar line at all times
Time escape attempts to the moment the attacker reaches for the second grip, when their posting ability is most compromised
Bridge toward the posted leg side when the attacker commits both hands to collar work, exploiting the reduced base stability
Never extend arms fully against the mounted opponent as this creates armbar and Americana vulnerabilities
recognition_cues: Opponent reaches cross-body toward your far collar with one hand while maintaining mount pressure with the other
Opponent uses head pressure against your jaw or cheek to turn your chin away, creating access to collar material on the exposed side
Opponent's weight shifts noticeably forward and their posted leg drives harder into the mat as they commit to the grip sequence
Opponent strips your defensive wrist control or swims past your frames specifically to access the collar rather than to establish arm control

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip strip using both hands to peel the first collar grip before the second is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you feel the first hand enter the collar, before the attacker consolidates the grip and removes slack
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker must re-establish grips from scratch, resetting the attack timeline and giving you time to set up escape sequences
defensive_options.risk: Both hands committed to grip fighting leaves your arms vulnerable to isolation for armbar or Americana attacks

defensive_options.action: Bridge toward posted leg side during second grip insertion when both attacker hands are off the mat
defensive_options.when_to_use: The moment the attacker reaches for the second collar with their free hand, eliminating their ability to post against the bridge
defensive_options.if_successful: Full reversal to guard position or top position, completely neutralizing the choke threat
defensive_options.risk: If the bridge fails, you have expended significant energy and the attacker may consolidate both grips during your recovery

defensive_options.action: Frame on biceps and shrimp escape toward the lighter side to create distance and recover guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has one grip but has not fully consolidated mount pressure, creating space for hip movement
defensive_options.if_successful: Create enough space to insert knee shield and recover half guard before the choke can be completed
defensive_options.risk: Frames may be defeated if attacker has superior weight distribution and walks hips higher in response

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with active collar control to deny access for the second grip
defensive_options.when_to_use: As a continuous defense throughout the choke attempt, particularly when the attacker uses head pressure to expose the collar
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker cannot complete the choke and may abandon the attempt or switch to a different submission
defensive_options.risk: Passive defense that does not improve position; attacker may switch to arm attacks while you focus on neck protection

escape_paths: Bridge toward posted leg side when attacker commits both hands to collar grips, driving through to achieve full reversal to closed guard
Elbow escape toward the lighter side during grip transitions, inserting knee shield to recover half guard before the choke is fully set

favorable_outcomes.how: Execute a well-timed bridge and roll when the attacker commits both hands to collar work, exploiting the reduced posting ability to achieve a full reversal to closed guard

common_errors.error: Pulling down on the attacker's wrists with fully extended arms
common_errors.consequence: Extended arms are immediately vulnerable to armbar, Americana, or wrist isolation attacks; the pulling motion provides no structural defense and accelerates energy expenditure
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows bent and tight to your body; use short, explosive grip-stripping motions with bent arms rather than extended pulling that exposes the joints

common_errors.error: Waiting until both collar grips are set before attempting any defensive action
common_errors.consequence: Once both collar grips are consolidated and deep, stripping them becomes nearly impossible; the choke will likely finish within seconds before any escape succeeds
common_errors.correction: Begin defensive action immediately when you feel the first hand entering the collar; the window for effective prevention closes rapidly after the first grip is set deep

common_errors.error: Panicking and bridging directly upward when the choke pressure begins
common_errors.consequence: Straight upward bridges from mount are easily absorbed; the energy expenditure accelerates the choke's effectiveness by increasing blood pressure and oxygen demand
common_errors.correction: Bridge at a 45-degree angle toward the posted leg side, targeting the weakest point of the attacker's base; combine the bridge with a turn toward the lighter side

common_errors.error: Neglecting chin position and allowing the chin to be turned away from the incoming second grip
common_errors.consequence: Exposed neck provides easy collar access for the second grip; once the chin is turned, the carotid artery on that side becomes directly accessible to the collar pressure
common_errors.correction: Actively fight to keep chin tucked to chest; use your hand nearest the threat to cup your own chin or press against the attacker's forehead to resist the chin turn

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a cross collar choke from 3-4 mount is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cues are the opponent reaching cross-body toward your far collar, their weight shifting forward as they commit to the grip, and head pressure against your jaw to turn your chin away. You may also feel their posted leg driving harder into the mat as they stabilize their base for grip insertion. Any hand entering the collar area from a cross-body angle while in mount signals a cross collar choke setup requiring immediate defensive action.

flashcards.question: What is the safest approach to tapping when caught in a cross collar choke from 3-4 mount?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately and clearly as soon as you feel choking pressure compressing your carotid arteries or when you recognize that both grips are set deep and you cannot strip them. Use a firm, repeated hand tap on the attacker's body or the mat, combined with a verbal tap saying 'tap.' Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness within 5-10 seconds of full application, so there is no benefit to enduring a fully locked choke. Tap early in training to protect long-term brain health.

flashcards.question: What defensive actions are available at each stage of the cross collar choke setup?
flashcards.answer: Before the first grip: maintain collar control with both hands, keep elbows tight, and use frames to prevent collar access. During first grip insertion: immediately apply two-on-one grip stripping with bent arms. Between first and second grip: bridge toward the posted leg side to exploit compromised base, or shrimp to create escape angle. After both grips are set: tuck chin hard, bridge and roll as a desperation attempt, or tap if the choke is locked. Defensive effectiveness drops dramatically at each stage, making early prevention essential.

flashcards.question: When is the optimal moment to attempt a bridge escape against the cross collar choke from 3-4 mount?
flashcards.answer: The optimal bridging moment is when the attacker reaches for the second collar grip with their free hand. At this instant, both of their hands are committed to collar work and they cannot post against a bridge. Their weight is typically shifting forward toward your head as they reach, raising their center of gravity. Bridge toward the posted leg side at this moment for the highest probability of a successful reversal, then immediately recover guard before they can reestablish position.

training_progressions.focus: Defending the first collar grip insertion before it sets
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts to insert first collar grip at 25% speed while defender practices collar control, hand fighting, and frame maintenance. Focus on recognizing the cross-body reach and intercepting it before the hand enters the collar. 20 repetitions per side with role switching.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying and exploiting the second-grip window for bridges
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes first collar grip and pauses before attempting the second. Defender practices the bridge toward the posted leg side during the second grip insertion at 50% resistance. Focus on timing the bridge to the exact moment the free hand leaves the mat for the collar.

training_progressions.focus: Applying all defensive tools against increasing intensity
training_progressions.description: Start with 25% resistance and build to 75% across rounds. Partner attempts the full cross collar choke sequence while defender uses all available defenses: grip stripping, bridging, framing, and chin tuck. Track which defense stage most frequently fails to identify training priorities.

training_progressions.focus: Defending under realistic pressure with mixed attacks
training_progressions.description: Full resistance positional sparring from 3-4 mount bottom. Bottom player scores for successful escapes, top player scores for submission or position advancement. Two-minute rounds with the choke as a genuine threat combined with other attacks to simulate competition pressure.
